results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 45 outline summaries match the controlling ideas of the aligned spec paragraphs p01-p45 in spec order; the three introduction callouts match no spec paragraph, as expected.

Adyen ¶4 (marked two_ideas) is one idea with two instances: the spec's controlling idea for p24 is 'two published mechanisms keep the books right despite the split', and the paragraph opens with exactly that sentence. All other units except Adyen ¶6 were summarised with one idea.

results.draft_locus: What Adyen Has Published: PostgreSQL, Accounting Clusters and Partitions ¶6
results.quote: One more store is named once. For API idempotency at its stateless edge, part one of the 2021 series says: “The information needs to be available locally, so we eventually decided on integrating Cockroach, a distributed database, with our PALs.”
results.finding: The paragraph joins two ideas: what Adyen has not published, and a published second store for idempotency keys with its vendor follow-up. The outliner needed two summaries and flow reader A read the Cockroach part as an afterthought. The spec's p26 controlling idea itself bundles both.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene and p09-p11 to C1; p12-p14 to C2; p15-p20 to C3; p21-p26 to C4; p27-p31 to C3/C4/C5; p32-p40 to C5; the conclusion lists to C1-C5. The partitioning paragraph (Adyen ¶5) traces to C4's 2023-2025 record, though its purpose is not stated (failed under evidence_is_explained and flow_is_followable).

The tables (requirements, shard placement, Where They Differ, four designs, Larkfield lag table), Figures 1-3 and most quotations are followed or framed by a sentence saying what they show (e.g. 'The habit is the same as in the shard move: copy, compare, then switch'; 'As I read it, sharding the books replaced ... with messages'; the two INFERENCE callouts).

results.draft_locus: What Adyen Has Published: PostgreSQL, Accounting Clusters and Partitions ¶5
results.quote: “I still have nightmares about incident number 2016. We were preparing for one of the most critical seasons for our merchants – December shopping– when the CPU unexpectedly spiked.” Adding one more partition would have overloaded one of its most critical databases. (“2016” is an incident number, not a year.)
results.finding: The incident quotation is followed only by a paraphrase and a note on the number; no sentence says what it shows for the chapter (the spec's 'shows': that dividing data inside one database still carries an operational cost). Both flow readers could not tell why it is there.

The transitions at p02-p05, p07-p34 except the section openers noted below, p36, p38-p45 express their declared relationships and pick up the declared known information (e.g. 'The previous chapter explains why that is not a contradiction'; 'Why not make the boundary larger, as Tom proposed?'; 'A boundary of one database is comfortable until the data no longer fits'; 'For a team with one database and one other system to inform, those four parts have a common name'; 'The store's own shape also had to change'). The house-format conclusion lists open with labels ('Established.', 'Depends on context.', 'The author's synthesis.') that state their relationship.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Paid, and Not Activated ¶1
results.quote: Larkfield is the fictional studio-software platform this book follows ([[meet-larkfield]]).
results.finding: Declared: example, carrying 'the claim that consistency depends on where the boundary is drawn' into 'a case in which no boundary had been drawn at all'. The section opens with a gloss of Larkfield and never picks up the boundary claim; the 'no boundary drawn' framing is left to the reader. Not covered by the waiver: this is the leading sentence, not the section's position.

results.draft_locus: What Stripe Has Published: A Document Database and a Platform That Moves Data ¶1
results.quote: Stripe's fullest account is the 2024 post already quoted.
results.finding: Declared: example, carrying 'the costs of sharding in general' into 'the first of two published accounts of living with them'. The opening picks up the introduction's quotation instead and does not connect the Stripe account to the costs of sharding just set out.

Both readers describe the post-level order as problem, concept, scale, evidence, comparison, inference, small-scale design, application, failure, which agrees with the declared problem_solution pattern and its prerequisite_order, comparison and large_to_small sub-patterns; both found every section's position clear except the points failed below, and both credit the roadmap.

results.finding: Both readers could not see why the 2017 schema-migration paragraph sits in the Stripe section; its purpose appears only about eighty lines later at Larkfield's migration. The spec's section flow deliberately keeps it here, so the difficulty comes from the order.

The introduction opens on a puzzling, sourced scenario (Stripe rejecting reads and writes for two seconds on purpose), bridges from the previous chapter, states a disputable thesis and gives a roadmap; none of the weak patterns applies.

The conclusion sorts the chapter's points into established, conditional and the author's synthesis, adds review questions and hands off by contrast; it does not open with 'in conclusion', introduce a new subtopic, hold body evidence or end on a rephrased thesis alone.

The synthesis bullets state what no single section states ('the database product matters less for money than the boundary ... what their accounts share is the discipline around the store'; 'consistent' is incomplete until it names the check and who looks at it), and the conditional list and eight questions say what a team does with it.

The conclusion returns to the two seconds under 'what it lets give way': 'under two seconds of rejected requests during a move at Stripe (2024)', framing the refusal as the relaxation chosen to keep the record right, as callback.how requires.

The intro reader predicted every section in order (scene, what must be exact, sharding, Stripe, Adyen, comparison and inference with what is not public, outbox at Larkfield, failures, hand-off), the kind of evidence (dated primary posts, Larkfield example, a comparison table, inference marked) and the careful declarative tone. It did not foresee the online-migration thread, which the spec's roadmap also omits (see flow_is_followable).

The cold reader gives the full expected answer: payment state and outbox row in one local transaction, a relay that repeats until acknowledged, a booking app that stores the event id in the same transaction so a repeat changes nothing, and a nightly comparison of paid payments against activated passes for the row that was never written.

results.draft_locus: What Adyen Has Published: PostgreSQL, Accounting Clusters and Partitions ¶3
results.quote: As I read it, sharding the books replaced what one database could do in one transaction with messages. The post does not describe them.
results.finding: The reader got the core: the debit is no longer one local transaction, money must move between clusters, Adyen's 'quite painful' and 'back and forth messages', and the protocol is not public. But the expected answer also has the reader add that such messages must be idempotent and verified; the reader only notes that a message 'can fail or arrive twice' and names no remedy. The Adyen passage ends on 'The post does not describe them' without tying the messages to idempotency and a later check, which the draft does only generically in the inference section.

The no-spanning-transaction claim is labelled as the author's inference in the introduction, in the key points, in an INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED callout and in the synthesis ('my inference from published mechanisms'); what is not public is listed for Stripe (¶6 of its section: data outside DocDB, transaction boundaries, read consistency, write acknowledgement, replication) and for Adyen (¶6: cluster count, cross-cluster atomicity, rebalancing, synchronous replication, failover).

Scale figures carry year and unit (Stripe: over five million queries per second, petabytes, 2,000+ shards, 2024; Adyen: 5,000+ transactions per second and 74 TB in 2018, hundreds of terabytes in 2021, 20TB tables in 2023), and the comparison row states 'Not comparable: different years and different units'.
